_activity: From a 4 to a 5: principles in tension
_licence: ORIGINAL, built on the 11.2 casefile documents (numbered per the signed 11.2 map). Quotes are the casefile's adapted text.
design_intent: Not skill practice. A kid here already writes at a 4. This is the gold dust that turns a 4 into a 5: more content, a wider lens, and a named technique.

tidbits.text: Your card sorts the 12 principles into three groups: how power is built and limited, where it comes from, and what government must protect. Asking which group you're in narrows the choice fast.
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) puts two principles against each other: Federalism (the nation versus a state) and Limited Government (can Congress do what the Constitution doesn't list?).
The Civic Literacy Essay asks you to name the principle at stake. A 5 doesn't just name it. It says whether the document upholds it, denies it, or fights over it.

exemplars.text: The Sedition Act was about Individual Rights because it punished people for speech.

The Sedition Act put Individual Rights (civil liberties) at stake: seven years after the First Amendment promised that Congress would make no law limiting freedom of speech or of the press, Congress jailed editors for criticizing the president, showing that a written right is only as strong as people's willingness to defend it.
exemplars.what_changed: The 4 names the principle. The 5 says it was fought over, shows the promise and the break side by side, and says what that proves.

techniques.name: Name it, then take a side
techniques.explanation: Name the principle from your card, then say: upheld, denied, or fought over. That's the whole Q4 move.

techniques.name: Show two principles pulling
techniques.explanation: Some moments put two principles against each other. Naming both shows you see the real argument.

try_it.prompt: Pick one principle from your card. Where did you see it in your own week, at school, at home, or at work?
try_it.status: Untimed, optional, never scored, never saved — practice reflection only.
